content: Burn injuries that involve a large total body surface area (TBSA) can lead to a state of systemic breakdown, resembling severe malnutrition. The destruction of the skin barrier in such cases results in impaired regulation of body temperature, increased susceptibility to infections, and significant fluid loss. Nutritional support is a cornerstone of managing severe burn injuries, and a specific approach called immunonutrition focuses on modulating immune system activity through targeted nutrients. Immunonutrition aims to address three key areas: maintaining mucosal barrier function, enhancing cellular defense mechanisms, and controlling local or systemic inflammation. The nutrients most commonly used in this context include glutamine, arginine, branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), omega-3 fatty acids (n-3 fatty acids, such as those found in fish oil), and nucleotides. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of a diet enriched with immunonutrients (such as glutamine, arginine, BCAAs, n-3 fatty acids, or combinations of these) compared to an isonitrogenous diet (a diet with the same overall protein content but different nutrient composition) on clinical outcomes in patients with severe burn injuries. The outcomes of interest included mortality, length of hospital stay, rates of burn wound infections, and rates of non-wound infections (such as bloodstream infections, pneumonia, and urinary tract infections). The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, with the initial search completed in August 2012 and an update performed in October 2014. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared the addition of immunonutrients to a standard nutritional regimen versus an isonitrogenous diet or another immunonutrient agent. Two authors independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with additional reviewers. A total of 16 trials involving 678 participants met the inclusion criteria and contributed data to the analysis. However, many of these studies did not adequately report their methods of randomization or adhere to intention-to-treat principles, which raises concerns about the reliability of the findings. Glutamine was the most frequently studied immunonutrient, used in seven of the 16 trials. Compared to an isonitrogenous control, glutamine supplementation was associated with a reduction in hospital length of stay (mean reduction of 5.65 days, 95% confidence interval [CI] -8.09 to -3.22) and a decrease in mortality (pooled risk ratio [RR] 0.25, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.78). However, due to the small sample sizes in these studies, these results may represent a false-positive effect. No evidence was found to suggest that glutamine had any impact on burn wound infections or non-wound infections. Similarly, other immunonutrients investigated in the trials showed no significant effects on mortality, hospital length of stay, or infection rates. The authors concluded that while there is some evidence suggesting that glutamine may reduce mortality in patients with severe burn injuries, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited number of participants and methodological concerns in the included studies. Larger, well-designed trials are needed to confirm the potential benefits of glutamine and to evaluate the effects of other immunonutrients in this patient population.
